narrative:
The model predicted a 60% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability exceeded the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is well below the average of roughly the middle of the class (5.8) among students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking in the second decile also pulled the prediction toward failure, though less dramatically; again this was noticeably lower than the average sixth-decile performance of accepted students.

Your LSAT score of 36 worked in the opposite direction. It was only slightly below the accepted-student average of 37.2, and this modest difference provided the main positive signal that the model interpreted as increasing your chance of passing. However, this encouraging factor was not large enough to outweigh the two academic-ranking signals.

Your family income, undergraduate GPA of 2.8 (versus 3.23 average), full-time study plans, gender, and race played no meaningful role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your class standing in the remaining law-school years and consider retaking the LSAT if you can realistically reach a higher score. These two areas offer the clearest path to shifting a future prediction in your favor. (218 words)
